la:noun:area.html:
ārĕa (in inscriptions freq. ARIA, , etc.), ae,
f [some comp. ἔραζε = on the ground; Germ. Erde; Engl. earth, hearth; others, as Varro and Festus, connected it with areo, as if pr. dry land, as terra may be connected with torreo; so Bopp and Curt.], a piece of level ground, a vacant place, esp. in the town (syn.: planities, aequor): in urbe loca pura areae, Müll: area proprie dicitur locus vacuus, Paul. ex Müll.: locus sine aedificio in urbe area; rure autem ager appellatur,.
Lit., ground for a house, a building-spot: si Ponendae domo quaerenda est area primum,. arearum electio, : pontifices si sustulerint religionem, aream praeclaram habebimus,; ; ; ; —
Transf.
A vacant space around or in a house, a court (syn. spatium): resedimus in areā domŭs,; so ; ; ; —
An open space for games, an open play-ground (syn.: campus, curriculum),.— Hence, in gen., a field for effort, etc. (syn.: campus, locus, q. v.),, and trop.: area scelerum,i. e. where vices have full scope,.—Also, a raceground, (cf. ); and trop., the course of life: vitae tribus areis peractis (i. e. pueritiā, juventute, senectute),.—
A threshing floor (among the ancients, an open space in the vicinity of the house).
Lit.: neque in segetibus neque in areis neque in horreis,; ; ; ; ; . Its construction may be learned from and 129; ; sqq. Voss; ; ; and —
Trop., of the body of Christians, as subject to separation, judgment (eccl. Lat.), ; .—
The halo around the sun or moon: tales splendores Graeci areas (i. e. ἅλωνας) vocavere, .—
A bed or border in a garden, Müll.; ; ; .—
A fowling-floor, : aedes nobis area est; auceps sum ego,.—
A burying-ground, church-yard, . —
A bald spot upon the head, baldness, ; .

ārĕo, ēre, v. n.
akin to ardere
,

Lit.: ubi (amurca) arebit,; : uti, quom exivissem ex aquā, arerem tamen,; : (tellus) sucis aret ademtis,; so .—
Trop. of things, to be dried up or withered: arentibus siti faucibus,; so : fauces arent,: aret ager,: pars, super quam non plui, aruit,: omnia ligna agri aruerunt, ib. Joel, 1, 12; ; .—Rarely of persons, to languish from thirst: in mediā Tantalus aret aquā,; so, Sic aret mediis taciti vulgator in undis,. —Hence, ārens, entis, P. a.
Lit., dry, arid, parched: saxa,: arens alveus (fluminis),: arva,: rosae,; : harenae,: cetera (loca) abrupta aut arentia, * . —
Trop., languishing or fainting from thirst, thirsty: trepidisque arentia venis Ora patent,; : faux,.—Poet. as an epithet of thirst itself: sitis,; (cf.: sitis arida,; ).

la:other:Arethusa.html:
Ărĕthūsa, ae, f., = Ἀρέθουσα.
A celebrated fountain near Syracuse, ; acc. to the fable, a nymph in the train of Diana, in Elis, pursued by the river-god Alpheus, fled to Sicily, (cf. Pausan. 5, 7); hence it was believed that it flowed under the sea with the Alpheus, and appeared again in Sicily, sqq.; ; ; ; cf. Mann. Ital. II. 325, and Alpheus.—
A fountain in Eubœa, .—
A fountain in Bœotia, .—
A lake in Armenia Major, (Jan, Aritissa).—
A town in Macedonia, .—
A town in Syria, on the Orontes, now Rustan or Restun, Itin. Anton. —
Derivv.
ărĕthūsaeus, a, um, adj., of or pertaining to the fountain Arethusa (in Sicily), Arethusian, .—
ărĕthūsis, ĭdis, adj., Arethusian, a poet. epithet for Syracuse, near which was the fountain Arethusa, (cf. : Aganippis Hippocrene).—
ărĕthūsĭus, a, um, adj.
Arethusian; hence poet. for Syracusan: proles,.—
Subst.: ărĕthūsĭi, ōrum, m.
The inhabitants of Arethusa, in Macedonia, .—
The inhabitants of Arethusa, in Syria, .

la:other:Ares.html:
Ăres, is, m., = Ἄρης,
the war-god Mars (in Plaut. jocosely made to correspond with bellator, warrior): si tu ad legionem bellator clues, at ego in culinā Ares,. (For the A, which is always short in Lat., cf. Lucil. ap. Scaur. Orth. p. 2255 P., and , with reference to Hom. Il. 5, 31.)

senses: to become dry, dry out
to wither (of plants)
to languish
la:verb:aresco.html:
āresco, ĕre,
v. n. inch. [areo], to become dry.
Lit.: dum mea (vestimenta) arescunt,: fluvius arescat,: arescat aqua de mari,: arescente undā,: quasi faenum, ita arescet,.—Of tears: cito arescit lacrima, praesertim in alienis malis,; so —
Trop., to languish.
Of plants, to dry up, wither: nullo modo facilius arbitror posse herbas arescere et interfici, to dry up, Cic. Oecon. ap. ; so : truncus (arboris),: vitis,; : palmes,: manus (branch), ib. Job, 15, 32.—
Of persons (eccl. Lat.), to pine away in sickness: (filius meus) stridet dentibus et arescit,.—So, to sink, be overcome, with fear: arescentibus hominibus prae timore,.
